newsitem.title: GERMANY: German banks face wrath of 30,000 steelworkers.
newsitem.headline: German banks face wrath of 30,000 steelworkers.

text.p: More than 30,000 steelworkers from Thyssen AG invaded Germany's financial capital on Tuesday to vent their anger at the role played by banks in a now-abandoned takeover bid by rival Krupp AG.

The workers swooped down from the industrial Ruhr region in a fleet of more than 200 buses and brought traffic in Frankfurt to a standstill as they marched in long columns into the banking district, blowing whistles, honking horns and chanting.

They waved banners which read "Crawl back into your safes" and "Banks - Hands Off Our Jobs." While the atmosphere was peaceful, workers made no secret of their fury at the role banks played in backing Krupp's takeover bid.

Some of them burnt their Deutsche Bank savings account books. "They're the biggest crooks alive," one Thyssen steelworker from Duisburg said. "They finance job cuts and the main thing is that they make their money."

Addressing a rally outside the glass-fronted twin towers of Deutsche Bank AG, Klaus Zwickel, the leader of the giant metal and engineering trade union IG Metall, lambasted banks for jeopardising workers' livelihood with "casino capitalism."
"We're signalling the resistance of society against the arrogance of banks and the despotism of financial capital," Zwickel told the rally.
Deutsche, Dresdner Bank AG and U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs had backed steel group Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp in its hostile bid for Thyssen AG.
After a storm of protest from unions and politicians against what they called "Wild West" tactics, Krupp called off its bid late on Monday.
But both firms said they would form a steel joint venture and explore expanding co-operation into other areas, a move which workers and union officials still fear could cost jobs.

Hostile takeover bids are common in Britain and the U.S. but rare in Germany because they go against the grain of a business and political culture based on seeking consensus between conflicting interests.
Thyssen's works council chairman said Tuesday's protest was aimed at preventing what he called the "Americanisation" of German society.

The banks have come under heavy fire for helping Krupp arrange the bid which was expected to cost thousands of jobs in the Ruhr region, Germany's industrial heartland, at a time when unemployment is at its highest level since the war.
The affair has also led to renewed calls for curbs on the power wielded by German banks through their large industrial shareholdings and their presence on many different company supervisory boards.
Deutsche bore the brunt of criticism because its management board member Ulrich Cartellieri is on Thyssen's supervisory board. He did not inform it of Krupp's impending bid.
The Frankfurt protest by steelworkers follow demonstrations two weeks ago by miners and construction workers against threatened job losses.
Deutsche Bank on Monday defended its role, saying it was normal for a bank to accept a mandate to arrange a takeover bid.
It also denied it was pursuing any industrial policy of its own and said it was willing to back any plan that secured jobs.
